name: Men's makeup (contour, bronzer, highlight)

lead: Subtle contour, highlighter and bronzer make the jaw, cheekbones and nose look more defined, so the face looks sharper while the makeup is worn.

Contouring uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin in hollows and along edges to create shadow, while highlighting uses lighter shades on prominent areas. It has roots in theatrical makeup, was popularised by a 2000 book, and went mainstream on social media in the 2010s.

paras: People apply a darker shade under the cheekbones and along the jawline, a lighter one on the high points, and blend until the edges disappear. Men usually keep it light so it reads as natural, and the effect is immediate.
Low risk. Makeup can irritate or break out sensitive skin, and heavy or poorly blended application is easy to spot.

social.title: Gen Z is making men's makeup go "mainstream." Gen X and the 1980s would like a word

chain: Darker shade in hollows, lighter on edges
Shadow and light change the face
angle.text: Darker shades in the hollows and lighter ones on prominent edges create shadow and light that make the jaw, cheekbones and nose look more defined. The effect is visible while worn and follows standard makeup practice.

lead: Men's contour, bronzer and highlight use shading and light to make the face look more defined. A shade one or two tones darker than the skin goes into the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create shadow and a slimmer, more sculpted look, while a lighter shade goes on prominent areas such as the cheek apples, nose tip and T-zone.[1] Bronzer adds warmth and depth to the skin overall. In looksmaxxing terms, the aim is a sharper jaw, higher-looking cheekbones and a straighter nose, achieved in minutes and washed off at the end of the day.

The technique comes from theatre and film. Elizabethan stage actors used chalk and soot so audiences could read their faces, Max Factor Sr. added shading so faces would not look flat on camera and presented a contouring tutorial for different face shapes in 1945, and Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward introduced sculpting to the general public.[1] Social media and dedicated contour and strobing products made it mainstream in the 2010s.[1]

Male cosmetics have a long history, from eye pigments in ancient Egypt to powdered skin in Elizabethan England, but were a niche market until the late 1990s.[2] Wikipedia reports that men aged 18 to 34 are more likely to use cosmetics, that men cite covering skin flaws and improving appearance as reasons, and that male beauty creators on YouTube have grown in number.[2] No published study has examined how contouring changes the perceived attractiveness of men.
infobox: Powder or cream contour palettes, highlighters, bronzer[1]

paras: Contouring places warm or cool darker shades in the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples to create a slimming, sculpted look. Highlighting uses lighter shades on the cheek apples, nose tip and T-zone, and strobing relies mainly on light shades with little or no darker shading.[1] Powder contour products are often sold as palettes with both light and dark shades, while cream products give a more emphasized look.[1]

Wikipedia describes contouring as a way to accentuate existing features or hide and change unwanted ones.[1] Bronzer is not covered in that article; it is generally used to add warmth to the skin and to shade the face's outer edges.

Wikipedia records men's cosmetic use across cultures, including dark eye pigments in ancient Egypt, powdered skin in Elizabethan England and the white base used by male kabuki actors.[2] Men's beauty products were scarce until the late 1990s.[2]

According to the same article, some men use concealer to cover acne marks and freckles and some use cosmetics to enhance their appearance, while older men use products to even out skin tone and reduce visible wrinkles and age spots.[2] It reports that only about 17 percent of men consider makeup important in daily life, though far more use skincare, and that men's packaging tends to use simpler, darker colours to reduce resistance to cosmetics.[2] Industry coverage has described Gen Z as pushing men's makeup toward the mainstream.[3]

Looksmax.org has threads on using bronzer and contour to change the apparent shape of the face, with users presenting them as a low-cost, non-permanent way to simulate stronger bone structure.[4] Supporters treat makeup as one of the style-oriented tools alongside grooming and hair, since the effect is optical and can be matched to lighting and camera angle. Others in the community regard makeup as outside the practice or prefer permanent changes such as fat loss or surgery.
No studies found. Published literature on male cosmetic contouring concerns surgical and device-based body contouring, which is a different subject.

lore.intro: Male contouring appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a cheap, reversible way to simulate stronger bone structure.[4]

claims.claim: Contour and bronzer can change the apparent shape of the whole face.
Makeup carries stigma for men that limits its use.

Film actors such as Marlene Dietrich use shading to accentuate facial lines.[1]
